grades.reason: Covers why an OS abstracts hardware resources (isolation, time-sharing, exec building a memory image). It never discusses why a shell forks before exec.
These are programming exercises about forker and a microshell, plus zombie reaping. They don't explain why a shell uses fork before exec.

grades.quote: Now it should be clear why it is helpful that fork and exec are separate calls: between the two, the shell has a chance to redirect the child’s I/O without disturbing the I/O setup of the main shell.
grades.reason: Directly explains why fork and exec are separate and why the shell runs exec in a forked child. Between the two calls the shell can redirect the child's I/O without disturbing its own I/O setup. It also shows the code and compares this with a hypothetical combined forkexec.

grades.quote: The same pattern of fork, execute, and wait would apply in any case where the forking of a child process is not to enable concurrency, but rather to provide a separate process context in which to run another program.
grades.reason: Explains that the shell forks a child, runs the program in the child, and the parent either continues (background) or waits. This gives a separate process context for the program. It never says outright that exec would replace the shell, though the execer example (same process became ps) implies it.
